Welcome toKepler's Equation

A planet circles its star on an ellipse: where is it at any given time?

About: Kepler's second law, the auxiliary circle and Kepler's equation ψ − e·sinψ = η

About this simulation

On screen
Left: the orbit, drawn to scale. The star is at the focus F, a distance ae from the centre C. A small ring on the auxiliary circle at angle η from C marks where a body going round that circle at a steady rate, in the same period, would be. The dashed auxiliary circle of radius a is the same size at every e. The body B sits on the ellipse directly above or below the point Q on the circle. ψ is the angle PCQ and θ is the angle PFB. The shaded region FPB is the area swept out since pericentre. A dot is left every twelfth of a period. Right: the true anomaly θ against t, with the dashed line of a circular orbit and, in faint grey, the curve for the previous eccentricity.
Controls
Eccentricity e, from 0 to 0.9. Changing it returns the body to pericentre with the clock at zero and pauses. The time slider drags t along one period and pauses the run. ▶ Play runs one period in 20 s.
Measured
t in units of the period. η, ψ and θ are in radians and r in units of a. All come from the exact solution of Kepler's equation (Newton–Raphson) at the clock time, and are grouped in the Readouts panel.
Assumptions
One body orbiting a star fixed at the focus, with the body's mass negligible and no other forces, so the orbit is an exact Kepler ellipse. For two comparable masses the same equations hold for their relative orbit.
Finding a Body on Its Ellipse
The orbit and its auxiliary circlewith θ against t beside it

Guided Inquiry

1 · Sweeping out area

Set the eccentricity to e = 0.6 and drag the time back to t = 0, so that the body is at pericentre. Before pressing play, predict how the shaded area FPB grows during the first half of the period. Then press play and watch it.

2 · A quarter of the period

Keep e = 0.6 and pause at pericentre. Before dragging the time to a quarter of the period, t = 0.25 Porb, predict the true anomaly θ there, where a body on a circle with the same period would have turned through η = π/2. The ¼ P chip under the time slider sets t exactly.

3 · Half the period

Keep e = 0.6. Before dragging the time on to half of the period, t = 0.5 Porb, predict where the body is then. The ½ P chip sets t exactly.

4 · Fast and slow

Keep e = 0.6, drag the time back to 0 and press play, watching the dots the body leaves at every twelfth of the period. Before it passes apocentre, predict how many times faster the true anomaly changes at pericentre than at apocentre.

5 · The near half at e = 0.8

Set the eccentricity to e = 0.8, which returns the body to pericentre. The half of the orbit nearer the star is the part with θ between −π/2 and π/2, to the right of the vertical line through F, and at θ = π/2 the dotted line from B to Q passes through F. Before pressing play, predict what fraction of the period the body spends on that half of the orbit.

6 · Summary: solving Kepler's equation

The body sweeps equal areas in equal times, so the mean anomaly η = 2πt/Porb grows steadily. Kepler's equation, η = ψ − e sin ψ, gives the eccentric anomaly ψ, the angle of Q on the auxiliary circle, and B lies directly above or below Q on the ellipse.

From ψ follow the true anomaly θ, with tan(θ/2) = √((1 + e)/(1 − e)) tan(ψ/2), and the distance r = a(1 − e cos ψ). An eccentric body rushes through pericentre and spends most of its period far from the star.

Finding a Body on Its Ellipse

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

This sim finds where a body is on its Kepler ellipse at any time. It builds the ellipse from a circle of the same size, and shows three angles, η, ψ and θ, that connect the clock to the place on the orbit.

What you'll learn

  • How the area swept out from pericentre relates to the time.
  • How one construction gives the three angles.
  • How Kepler's equation turns a time into a place.
  • How the eccentricity changes the time spent in each part of the orbit.
The construction: centre C, star at the focus F, pericentre P, body B on the ellipse, Q on the circle above it.

What's on screen

  • Cyan ellipse: the orbit, with the star at the focus F. The shaded region FPB is the area swept out since pericentre; dots mark every twelfth of the period.
  • Dashed circle: the auxiliary circle, radius a. The blue body B is joined by a dotted line to Q, the point on the circle above or below it. A dotted vertical line runs through F.
  • Amber ring η: where a body going round the circle at a steady rate, in the same period, would be.
  • Right and sidebar: the plot of θ against t, and the readouts t, η, ψ, θ and r/a.
See itLook at the orbit a tenth of the way round. Watch for: the star F off-centre, Q on the dashed circle, and B on the ellipse directly below it.

03

Equal areas in equal times, so the swept area is proportional to t

Kepler's second law says the line from the star to the body sweeps out equal areas in equal times. So the shaded area FPB, measured from pericentre, is proportional to t. The whole ellipse, of area πa²√(1 − e²), is swept in one period Porb.

That gives a steady clock. The mean anomaly η is the angle a body would have swept since pericentre if it went round the auxiliary circle at constant angular speed, with the same period. The sim marks that place with the amber ring.

Equation (2.9). t is measured from pericentre.
Key idea. The area swept since pericentre is the same fraction of the ellipse as the time is of the period. η is a measure of time, not a position on the ellipse.
See itWatch t run from 0 to 0.5 at e = 0.6. Watch for: the shaded region FPB growing until, at t = 0.500 Porb, it is exactly half of the ellipse.
04

Kepler's equation links the clock to the circle: ψ − e sin ψ = η

Put the origin at C, with the x-axis along CP. The ellipse is the auxiliary circle squeezed in the y-direction by √(1 − e²). So B lies directly above or below Q, with the same x: Q = (a cos ψ, a sin ψ), B = (a cos ψ, a√(1 − e²) sin ψ), and the star is at (ae, 0).

The squeeze multiplies every area by √(1 − e²) and leaves F and P in place. So area FPB is √(1 − e²) times the region FPQ: the sector CPQ, ½a²ψ, less the triangle CFQ, ½a²e sin ψ.

FPQ is the sector minus the triangle. The squeeze turns Q into B and FPQ into FPB.
Equation (2.12).

Setting this equal to the swept area ½a²√(1 − e²) η gives Kepler's equation (2.13):

For e < 1 each η gives exactly one ψ, but no elementary formula gives it, so the sim solves it numerically.
See itLook at a very eccentric orbit, e = 0.9. Watch for: the dotted line from B to Q vertical, with B at 0.436 of the height of Q above the axis.
05

Four steps from the clock to the body

Kepler's equation gives ψ. The other two quantities follow from the same construction (notes 2.10 to 2.15). The body is found in four steps: η from t by (2.9); ψ from η by (2.13); then r and θ from ψ:

Equation (2.11): the distance from the star.
Equation (2.15), with θ and ψ in the same half of the orbit.
e t

These sliders move the sim too, and follow it while it runs.

At e = 0.6 and t = ¼ Porb, η = 1.57 rad but ψ = 2.09 and θ = 2.58: the angle at the star is well ahead of the clock. At t = ½ Porb, ψ = π solves Kepler's equation for every e, since π − e sin π = π. Then θ = η = π: the body is at apocentre and the lead has gone.

See itSet the clock to a quarter of the period at e = 0.6. Watch for: η reading 1.57 rad while ψ reads 2.09 and θ reads 2.58.
See itNow take e = 0.9 to half a period. Watch for: η, ψ and θ all reading 3.14 rad, with B at the far end of the major axis.
06

Fast near pericentre, slow near apocentre, by the square of the distance

The area swept per unit time is ½r² dθ/dt. Equal areas in equal times therefore make r² dθ/dt constant, and the angle at the star changes as 1/r²: quickest at pericentre, slowest at apocentre.

Putting ψ = 0 and ψ = π in (2.11) gives rp = a(1 − e) and ra = a(1 + e). The ratio of the angular rates is (ra/rp)² = ((1 + e)/(1 − e))². At e = 0.6 that is 4² = 16; at e = 0.8 it is 9² = 81.

The dots are left a twelfth of a period apart. Equal times, so they spread out where the body turns quickly and crowd together where it turns slowly. The plot of θ against t is steep near t = 0 and flat near ½ Porb.

Key idea. The body's speed along its path and its distance from the star change together, so that r² dθ/dt stays fixed. The angle is not a clock.
See itWatch the dots appear as t runs from 0 to 0.5 at e = 0.6. Watch for: the first dots far apart near P, and later ones crowding together towards the far end of the ellipse.
07

At e = 0.8 the near half of the orbit takes about a twentieth of the period

The half of the orbit nearer the star is the part with θ between −π/2 and π/2, to the right of the dotted vertical line through F. At θ = π/2 the body stands straight above F, so the dotted line from B to Q passes through F.

There cos θ = 0, so (2.15) gives cos ψ = e and sin ψ = √(1 − e²). Kepler's equation then fixes the clock:

η = arccos e − e√(1 − e²), equation (2.16). At e = 0.8 this is 0.1635 rad, so t = η/2π = 0.026 Porb.

The body is at θ = −π/2 just as early before pericentre. So the whole near half takes 2η/2π = 0.052 of the period, about a twentieth, equation (2.17). For comparison, it takes 0.14 at e = 0.6, and exactly 0.5 at e = 0, where the orbit is a circle.

See itSet e = 0.8 and the clock to t = 0.026. Watch for: B standing on the dotted vertical line through F, with θ reading 1.57 rad.
08

Where it matters

  • Binary stars. A table of a body's positions at a series of times is called an ephemeris. The notes build one from these steps, and then place each position in space from a, e, i, Ωn and ω.
  • Comets. Halley's comet has e ≈ 0.97, beyond this sim's range. Its 76-year orbit is so lopsided that it spends only a few months of it on the half nearer the Sun.
  • Orbit software. Programs that give the position of a planet or satellite at a given time solve Kepler's equation numerically, every time.
Go deeper: how ψ is found

The notes use Newton–Raphson, starting from ψ0 = η (2.14):

The denominator 1 − e cos ψ is never zero for e < 1, so every step is defined. For e close to 1, starting from ψ0 = π is often safer.
09

Summary

In one line. The body's place on its ellipse follows from the time in four steps: η from t, ψ from Kepler's equation ψ − e sin ψ = η, then r and θ from ψ.

Key points

  • The area swept since pericentre is proportional to t, so η = 2πt/Porb is a steady clock.
  • Each η gives one ψ, found numerically; then r and θ follow.
  • r² dθ/dt is constant, so θ changes as 1/r², far faster at pericentre than at apocentre.

Common mix-ups

  • "A quarter of the period is a quarter of the angle." That holds for η, the clock angle. At e = 0.6 the body has already turned θ = 2.58 rad.
  • "The body lingers near the star, where gravity is strongest." It is quickest there. At e = 0.8 it covers the half nearer the star in 0.052 of the period.
  • "Kepler's equation gives θ directly." It gives ψ. Then r and θ follow from ψ.

Things to try on your own

  • Set e = 0 and press the ¼ P chip: η, ψ and θ agree.
  • Set e = 0.9 and press the ½ P chip: r/a reads 1.90, the apocentre distance (1 + e)a.

The plot of θ against t is Figure 11 of the notes.
